messages.author: b82af643aafe86d2
messages.subject: ODE solution when you know dydt, not y
parts:
I suspect this is easy, but I don't see the answer in the manual, and I haven't seen it in my searches yet, either.

Say you have a first-order ODE representing, for example, a river's catch basin.  You have measurements of precipitation, and you have measurements of river flow.  You don't have measurements of the water stored in the ground in that catch basin.  Simplistically, you model this with one state variable representing the stored water, and you model the outflow as an exponential; that is, dydt = -lambda * y.

How do you represent that in Stan's ODE solver?  I think precipitation becomes x_r, and y (the output of integrate_ode()) becomes stored water, but I'm totally unclear where dydt (river flow) fits in.

Thanks,

Bill

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] ODE solution when you know dydt, not y
parts:
If you have measurements of dy_dt then you don’t need to solve the ODE at all.
You just treat the stored water, y, as a latent variable.  Then conditioned on the
latent stored water the river slow is known exactly, dy_dt = - lambda * y, and then
you can add measurement noise.  So, for example,

data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  real<lower=0> flow_measurements[N];
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0> stored_water;
  real<lower=0> lambda;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}

transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> river_flow;
  river_flow <- -lambda * stored_water;
}

model {
  // need a prior for stored_water
  // need a prior for lambda
  // need a prior for sigma
  flow_measurements ~ normal(river_flow, sigma);
}

How precipitation fits in depends on your water model — for example stored_water
could itself be a function of precipitation.
On Dec 16, 2015, at 10:08 AM, Bill Harris <bill_...@facilitatedsystems.com> wrote:

I suspect this is easy, but I don't see the answer in the manual, and I haven't seen it in my searches yet, either.

Say you have a first-order ODE representing, for example, a river's catch basin.  You have measurements of precipitation, and you have measurements of river flow.  You don't have measurements of the water stored in the ground in that catch basin.  Simplistically, you model this with one state variable representing the stored water, and you model the outflow as an exponential; that is, dydt = -lambda * y.

How do you represent that in Stan's ODE solver?  I think precipitation becomes x_r, and y (the output of integrate_ode()) becomes stored water, but I'm totally unclear where dydt (river flow) fits in.

Thanks,

Bill

Thanks to both of you for your quick responses.  If it's as easy as you suggest, great, but I think I have some work to do to make Michael's model work (river_flow and stored_water are vectors / arrays).

In this case, I never have observations for y, but Michael's approach seems to miss the state variable concept--precipitation adds directly to stored_water, and, absent any precipitation, both river_flow and stored_water will exhibit exponential decay.  What am I missing?

Think capacitor charged by a programmable current source and discharged by a resistor.  I can only measure the current source and the current through the resistor.

Yes, I know the model isn't perfect; for one, I think there's a "dielectric absorption" piece that I may have to add.

When I get a minute--later today or tomorrow?--I'll try to work with it a bit more.

Bill

messages.author: b82af643aafe86d2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] ODE solution when you know dydt, not y
parts:
You're right, of course.  I was thinking / hoping that I could infer when the stored water / charge was 0 by observing when the outflow (river flow or current through the resistor) was 0, giving me y(To), not y(0), but I realize that it's hard to measure accurately when the flow goes to 0 (the slope of the stored water / charge over time is pretty shallow when the stock approaches 0).  

So I'm looking at hydrology examples using other packages now (actually, I've been sidetracked onto something else temporarily, but that's what I'm planning).

Still, I wonder if I'm slow or the problem still exists.  What if I have a general ODE problem with inflows and outflows, and I know sufficient initial or boundary conditions?  On top of the initial or boundary conditions on y (e.g., the value of y at some point To), I know dydt vs. t, not y vs. t.  I think I can model and solve that in MCSim, since the entire ODE model is in the main MCSim code (actually in the Dynamics {} block), but the ODE mechanics in Stan seems localized to a function with predefined signature.  

I was going to try that in MCSim before posting this, but I may not get back to this problem in the next day or three.  Still, it seems like a reasonable PBPK problem: it's cheap to measure when you give drugs and how much you give, but it's costly (in dollars and perhaps pain) to measure concentrations in plasma or other locations.  Are there example PBPK problems done in Stan to review?

Bill
